item.title: [heavy.com] What Is Going On With Jazz Chisholm Jr.? Why Is He Out Of Yankees Lineup Again?
item.dc:creator: Ben Stinar

item.content:encoded:
On Friday, the New York Yankees will open up their final series of the 2026 regular season.
They have a doubleheader with the Baltimore Orioles in the Bronx.
Underdog MLB wrote (on Friday): “Orioles-Yankees will move Saturday’s game to a doubleheader on Friday due to weather.”
The Yankees are coming off a 6-4 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday (also in the Bronx).
Jazz Chisholm Jr. did not play.
Lineup For Game 1
For the first game on Friday, the Yankees have announced their starting lineup.
FantasyPros wrote: “NYY Yankees Lineup 09/25 Game 1 1. Paul Goldschmidt 1B 2. Ben Rice DH 3. Heliot Ramos LF 4. Amed Rosario RF 5. George Lombard SS 6. Spencer Jones CF 7. Anthony Volpe 3B 8. Ali Sanchez C 9. Jose Caballero 2B”
Chisholm Jr. remains out of the lineup on Friday.
The two-time MLB All-Star recently returned from the injured list.
He is batting .233 with 109 hits, 19 home runs, 55 RBIs, 69 runs and 41 stolen bases in 136 games this year.
It’s fair to assume that Chisholm Jr. will likely be back in the lineup on Friday night (for the second game).
Social Media Reacts To Jazz Being Out Of Lineup
Here’s what people were saying:
@Santo_Tripp: “Nastiest part of Volpe being at 3rd, surprisingly isn’t that they chose to do the experiment, it’s the fact that jazz isn’t even in the lineup. AND THAT’S THE WHOLE REASON HE IS BEING TRIED OUT AT THIRD!!!!”
@yanksjazz: “Is it possible Jazz will not play in round 1? Sox will throw 2 lefties”
@disyanks: “Sitting Jazz just long enough to make sure he’s cold against Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray? Boone is an idiot”
@rickcarter12: “Don’t need Jazz or McMahon since Red Sox will be starting lefties…Yanks can’t beat Gray or Tolle anyway..even when they had Judge and Stanton”
Looking At The Yankees
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with a 92-67 record in 159 games.
They are 45-33 in 78 games at home.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Anthony Volpe decision got tougher after one huge swing

item.content:encoded:
For six innings Thursday, the Yankees trailed Tampa Bay 4-0. By the end of the eighth, George Lombard Jr. had turned the game around with a two-run homer. New York won 6-4, and the rookie finished 2-for-4 with a double, a homer and three RBI.
The comeback was fun. The shortstop question it leaves behind is less comfortable. Lombard also drove in a run with a seventh-inning double, then hit the decisive ball an inning later. He is giving the Yankees useful at-bats at the exact point they have to think about their October roster.
Anthony Volpe played Thursday and scored during the seventh-inning rally, but went 0-for-3 with a walk. One game does not settle his place on the roster. Lombard's growing body of work does make it harder to treat shortstop as a job Volpe gets back automatically.
Yankees can't ignore the at-bats Lombard is giving them
Lombard's homer was his seventh of the season. The number alone is not the argument for him. It is the way he has handled meaningful plate appearances while playing shortstop every day. In Thursday's win, he produced the first extra-base hit of the comeback and the last one that mattered.
The postseason roster discussion has included both Lombard and Volpe, but the club has not announced its choice. I would keep Lombard at shortstop if the Yankees opened a playoff series tomorrow. I am judging their current play, not closing the door on Volpe's future here.
0What do you think?Post a comment.
A good problem with a real consequence
The Yankees have enough infield options to find Volpe playing time if they want it. The harder decision is who starts at shortstop in a close playoff game. Lombard gave them another answer Thursday, and Rice's recent power surge has made this lineup look deeper than it did a month ago. There is no need to decide the entire October card today. Lombard has earned the chance to keep making that decision difficult.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Analyzing Whether Yankees' Anthony Volpe Third Base Experiment Could Actually Work?
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno; Unknown
item.description: As the New York Yankees try to sort out the final pieces of their playoff plan throughout this relatively meaningless final week of the regular season, there's one position that's quickly gaining interest and intrigue: third base. Ryan McMahon has gotten the lion's share of reps there over the course of the season, especially after the team began reducing the usage of a struggling Amed Rosario, whose bat and glove seemed to regress heavily in the offseason. José Caballero took over the position
item.content:encoded:
As the New York Yankees try to sort out the final pieces of their playoff plan throughout this relatively meaningless final week of the regular season, there's one position that's quickly gaining interest and intrigue: third base.
Ryan McMahon has gotten the lion's share of reps there over the course of the season, especially after the team began reducing the usage of a struggling Amed Rosario, whose bat and glove seemed to regress heavily in the offseason. José Caballero took over the position during McMahon's brief stint on the injured list, but has mostly ceded it back since.
However, Wednesday night's game notwithstanding, McMahon has struggled mightily offensively, so much so that he might be forcing the Yankees' hand. It doesn't help his case that he's regressed from a Gold Glove-caliber defender to a merely average one.
With McMahon's struggles, the Yankees have opened the door for someone else to take the position in October. While the most likely candidate is Caballero, Aaron Boone revealed Wednesday that an unlikely candidate is emerging: Anthony Volpe.
This could just be to have him ready as a depth option, but it could also be a sign that the team is weighing whether he could give the team the best chance to win at third base. There's reason to believe he can, but also reason to believe it might not be a good idea.
Why Anthony Volpe at third base may work
The simplest reason that it may work is that Volpe is a naturally gifted defender.
In three of his four years in the major leagues, he has graded out positively defensively while playing almost exclusively at the most demanding position, both in terms of range and arm strength.
In 2023, 2024, and 2026 combined, he had 25 Defensive Runs Saved, 21 Outs Above Average, and a 14 Fielding Run Value at the position while playing every day, three marks that were towards the top of the league.
The lone season he was not a good defender was 2025, when he played through a torn labrum for much of the season after an ill-fated dive on his non-throwing arm in May of that year. The immediate bounce-back after he returned from labrum surgery this season is proof that it wasn't spontaneous regression, but rather a fluke.
Still, with George Lombard Jr. grading out even better at shortstop in the minor leagues, Volpe was demoted in early August and asked to try other positions, which he's done since. In 93 innings at second base since being promoted back to the majors, he has 2 DRS and 1 OAA, looking clean and crisp throughout.
But what about third base? Most players who can handle shortstop tend to be even better at second and third base, something that the front office definitely hoped with Volpe after moving him off the position this summer. If he's good at shortstop, how great can he be elsewhere?
His range is undoubtedly his best attribute. Since coming into the league in 2023, Volpe has registered 10 runs of value off his range, which is higher than his actual total FRV of 8. If you remove his compromised 2025 data, he has 15 FRV worth of range value, while his arm and ability to turn double plays are both in the negatives.
So at third base, there's no doubt that Volpe would be very good at knocking down balls and snagging them to his left and right, potentially giving the Yankees a weapon to prevent doubles down the left field line.
But the fact that his arm has been a big negative at shortstop in his career will give some people pause about how good he can be at third base, a position that typically yields a bunch of long throws. That begs the question: does it matter?
Does arm strength matter at third base?
10 years ago, we'd have nothing but our eyes to determine how hard a guy can throw the ball. Fortunately, we have Statcast to help us now.
Volpe's arm strength has consistently been mediocre throughout his career, averaging between 81 and 82 miles per hour on his throws entering this year, when it has undoubtedly dipped due to the sample size at an easier position, per Baseball Savant. That mark consistently sat in the 30th percentile, well below average.
The average speed of a shortstop's throw in the majors is 86.2 mph. The average speed for a third baseman is 84.9 mph. It immediately dispels the belief that a third baseman has to have an equally strong arm, but where would Volpe stack up among those third basemen?
At 81-82 mph, Volpe would comfortably be below average at third base too, sliding in just above Kazuma Okamoto. Of the 53 third basemen with at least 50 throws, Volpe would be 38th.
How are the third basemen in his range defensively? Here are the 2026 defensive stats for the seven players in Volpe's immediate range:
Hao-Yu Lee: -3 DRS, -6 OAA, -4 FRV
Max Muncy (LAD): 3 DRS, 0 OAA, 1 FRV
Kazuma Okamoto: 2 DRS, -3 OAA, -3 FRV
Alex Bregman: 15 DRS, 9 OAA, 7 FRV
Max Muncy (ATH): -11 DRS, -6 OAA, -5 FRV
Brett Baty: 2 DRS, 1 OAA, 1 FRV
Caleb Durbin: 13 DRS, 5 OAA, 5 FRV
As you can see, it's an extreme mixed bag. Bregman and Durbin are two of the best defenders in baseball at their position despite not having a lot of zip on their throws, while Hao-Yu Lee and the Athletics' Max Muncy have been quite bad.
The fact that we have players from all different walks of life here suggests that arm strength doesn't matter nearly as much as some may believe. If a player has good range (the big calling cards of Durbin and Bregman), they can make up for maybe having to bounce a few. If they don't, it becomes a double negative.
It might also help to have a good first baseman at scooping. Paul Goldschmidt is one of the best of his generation at it (and this is now a Statcast stat!), but Luis García Jr. is quite mediocre. That said, the A's Nick Kurtz is significantly better at it than Boston's Willson Contreras and Chicago's Michael Busch.
So maybe arm strength just doesn't matter? If the Yankees deem that it isn't an issue, there should be no reservations about potentially deploying Volpe there come playoff time.

item.content:encoded:
Judge hopes to be ready for playoffs and Stanton could return for Yankees after 5 1/2-month absence
NEW YORK (AP) — Yankees slugger Aaron Judge hopes to return from a strained right calf for the playoffs next week and Giancarlo Stanton could be back after a 5 1/2-month absence.
New York manager Aaron Boone repeated he’s not counting on Judge to play in the AL Wild Card Series opener Tuesday. Judge, sidelined since Sept. 16, said he’s trying to do all he can to be in the lineup.
“The Bronx is a magical place in October,” Judge said after Wednesday night’s 9-2 win over AL East champion Tampa Bay. “I don’t want to miss out on that opportunity.”
Judge had a platelet-poor plasma injection Monday. He was sidelined by a fractured rib from May 31 to Sept. 8 and played in just seven games before the latest injury.
“Any injection doesn’t feel too good that day, but I feel a lot better today and we’re going to keep making strides,” he said.
A three-time AL MVP, Judge is hitting .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS in 66 games this season, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs since coming back from the rib injury.
“We are going to listen to the body and see how he heals,” Boone said. “If he is in a position to do that, obviously we are going to want him. So, no, I haven’t ruled anything out, of course.”
Boone said Tuesday he wasn’t planning on having Judge available for next week’s best-of-three series, likely against Boston.
“Obviously as a player, you don’t want to hear that but that’s out of my control,” Judge said.
Boone said Judge had a moderate strain.
“Everybody’s `moderate’ is a little different,” Judge said.
Stanton, trying to return from injuries to calf muscles in both legs, faced pitchers Wednesday at Double-A Somerset along with center fielder Trent Grisham, sidelined since straining his right hamstring on Sept. 4. Both ran the bases and Stanton homered while taking six or seven at-bats.
“Putting them on the outskirts of the conversation,” Boone, bothered by a cold, said in a raspy voice.
Following the end of the seasons for Yankees farm teams, New York has minor leaguers working out at Somerset in nearby New Jersey.
Stanton hasn’t played since April 24 because of strained calf muscles in both legs after starting the season with a .256 batting average, three homers and 14 RBIs in 24 games. The 36-year-old former NL MVP had 38 homers and 100 RBIs in his first season with New York in 2018 but has missed 500 of 1,194 games since (41.9%), through the end of this regular season.
His other injuries included strains of his right biceps, right knee, left hamstring (three times), left quadriceps and both calf muscles along with right ankle inflammation, left Achilles tendinitis and tendon pain in both elbows.
“You’re looking more at a pinch-hit scenario,” Boone said. “We’ll see if that’s even a realistic option.”
Stanton is owed $25 million next year in the final guaranteed season of a $325 million, 13-year contract that includes a $10 million buyout of a 2028 club option.
Lagrange could be brought up for major league debut
Carlos Lagrange, a 23-year-old right-hander who reached 100 mph with 98 pitches at Triple-A this year, threw to batters at Somerset. He was out between June 28 and Sept. 16 because of a right capsule strain.
Lagrange was shifted to the bullpen at the start of June.
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said.
Clarke Schmidt still out
Right-hander Clarke Schmidt, who returned Sept. 16 following Tommy John surgery in July 2025, played catch but remains sidelined by right biceps cramps. New York had hoped to use him as a reliever in the postseason.
“Today was better than yesterday,” Boone said. “If he’s not a real viable option by tomorrow, then we’ll probably go a different way.”
Postseason rotation
Boone said Cam Schlitter will start Game 1 or 2 of the playoffs. Max Fried appears set to start whichever game Schlittler doesn’t, with Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón available for Game 3.
“Whoever goes 1 or 2 can pitch 2 and 5 in the next series,” Boone said.
Fernando Cruz throws a bullpen
Right-hander Fernando Cruz threw a bullpen this week and is to throw another one Thursday.
He hasn’t pitched in a game since Aug. 25 because of right elbow discomfort caused by a partially torn ulnar collateral ligament.
“I’m in a really good position to be back I will say in the next couple of weeks,” Cruz said.
He took issue with the diagnosis of his injury.
“I had a real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” he said. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart it’s not a partial tear.”
Volpe will see time at the hot corner
With second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. back from a sprained right thumb, Boone said Anthony Volpe will see time at third.
“I’ll probably get him on there a time or two,” Boone said.
Volpe entered Wednesday hitting .263 with one homer, seven RBIs and four stolen bases over 11 games since his recall from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. He played three games at third base for the RailRiders.
“It didn’t feel that bad when I played there, but we’ll see,” Volpe said.
___

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

24 Sep 2026, 07:55 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Ryan McMahon hit a third-inning grand slam and tied a career high with five RBIs, while Ben Rice hit a pair of solo homers as the host New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night.
McMahon drove in five runs for the fourth time in his career and started his big night with a two-strike single off Tampa Bay spot starter Mason Englert (0-4) for a 2-0 lead in the second.
After George Lombard Jr. started the third with a homer to right-center field, McMahon lifted a full-count offering down the right field line for a 7-0 lead.
It was the third baseman's third career grand slam, and McMahon went deep after Anthony Volpe took ground balls at third before the game.
Rice homered on the first pitch of the contest from Englert to become the 13th Yankee with 40 homers in a season. After hitting his fourth career leadoff homer, Rice homered again into the right field seats for an 8-1 lead in the fourth.
Rice had his fifth career multi-homer game and became the seventh player to reach 40 homers this season. Rice also added a single and reached base four times.
The Yankees (91-67) won for the 10th time in 15 games. Rookie Spencer Jones doubled and scored on McMahon's RBI single in the second, while Heliot Ramos chipped in a sacrifice fly.
New York's Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed two runs on three hits in 5 2/3 innings in a postseason tuneup. Cole struck out eight, walked three and reached double-digit victories for the 10th time in his career.
Jonny DeLuca hit an RBI double, and Cedric Mullins homered for the Rays (96-62), who fell three games behind Milwaukee for the best record in baseball.
After clinching their fifth AL East title on Tuesday, the Rays rested AL hits leader Yandy Diaz and played Junior Caminero for five innings.
Englert allowed eight runs on nine hits over 3 2/3 innings after Ian Seymour was originally slated to start for Tampa Bay. Seymour is expected to pitch in Thursday's series finale.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Giancarlo Stanton, Carlos Lagrange, Game 1 starter among Yankees’ many playoff puzzle pieces
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while. “There’s a lot
item.content:encoded:
The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while.
“There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days,” the manager said before the Yankees played the division-winning Rays on Wednesday. “Hopefully, we have a lot of options to choose from.”
THE RETURN OF STANTON (AND GRISHAM)?
Giancarlo Stanton, out since April 24 due to three separate calf strains (two right, one left), and Trent Grisham, sidelined by his second right hamstring strain of the season, took live at-bats in Somerset on Wednesday. Both ran the bases, and Boone said Stanton homered while getting six or seven at-bats.
“They’re knocking on the door,” Boone said, but he wasn’t sure if Stanton, a decorated postseason performer, could be ready for the Wild Card round.
The manager previously said that Grisham could be in play, though he wasn’t expected to be activated before the final five games of the regular season.
Asked what he would need to see from Stanton after a five-month layoff, Boone earnestly said, “I’m not sure.”
“I don’t know that answer,” he continued. “Obviously, there’ll be conversations with him. Does he fit on the roster? Is it realistic? All those things, and I can’t answer that right now.”
With the Yankees already log-jammed with first-base/DH types — Stanton can’t play the outfield anymore — Boone added that the former MVP would probably be used as a pinch-hitter, if anything. While not a big role, Stanton’s right-handed bat could be helpful off the bench if the Yankees face the lefty-heavy Red Sox, their likeliest opponent, in the Wild Card round.
Grisham, meanwhile, would give the Yankees an interesting choice in center field with Spencer Jones handling the position in his absence. Jones has outperformed Grisham at the plate, but both are shaky defenders, and the latter has postseason experience that the rookie does not.
LAGRANGE TO DEBUT?
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said of flamethrowing pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange, who threw live batting practice on Wednesday.
But the skipper noted that a lot of “unknown” comes with righty, who has yet to make his major league debut, only recently returned from a shoulder sprain, and has just eight relief appearances under his belt this season. If the Yankees were to use Lagrange and his 100-plus-mph fastball, it would be out of the bullpen.
Asked why the Yankees don’t just promote Lagrange now, Boone said that they still have to cover innings over the last few games of the regular season. They would also have to clear space for him on the 40-man and active rosters.
While Lagrange is 23 and Stanton is 36, both are in similar positions in that they offer the Yankees an intriguing combination of upside, mystery and risk. Asked how Boone might personally weigh all that as the Yankees prepare to make their postseason roster, he said the club will “make the best decision possible” “if those guys are truly pushing into the conversation.”
“Carlos is in the stay ready [phase]. G [got] at-bats today,” Boone said. “All, at least, putting them on the outskirts of the conversation, if nothing else.”
WHO STARTS GAME 1?
Cam Schlittler is the clear frontrunner to win the American League Cy Young Award. So he’s obviously going to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round, right?
“Not necessarily,” Boone said. “We’ll see. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 doesn’t affect the next series. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 can pitch Game 2 and Game 5 in the next series, for example. We’ll decide what makes the most sense, just matching up how we want to go with it. But Cam would certainly be one of those first two games.”
Gerrit Cole, who totaled two earned runs, three walks and eight strikeouts over 5.2 innings and 105 pitches on Wednesday against the Rays, is currently lined up for Game 1 of the Wild Card round on extra rest. The 2023 Cy Young winner, now 22 starts removed from Tommy John surgery, has struggled to get swing-and-miss this season. He’s also faltered against the Red Sox throughout his career. With Max Fried and Carlos Rodón also in the rotation, the case can be made that Cole has been the Yankees’ fourth-best starter lately.
Schlittler, who dominated Boston in last year’s Wild Card series, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1. He is scheduled to make his final start of the regular season on Thursday.
VOLPE AT THIRD? MCMAHON OFF THE ROSTER?
With the lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon putting the finishing touches on an abysmal offensive season and taking a step back defensively, the righty-hitting Anthony Volpe did some pregame work at third base on Wednesday. Boone expects the shortstop turned second baseman to play the hot corner in one or two games before the regular season ends.
“Good to go,” Volpe, who played a few games at third in the minors this year, said of his comfort level at the position.
Meanwhile, José Caballero, another righty, has already gotten some starts at third over McMahon against right-handed pitching. If Volpe shows that he can handle third, it could increase the odds of the Yankees leaving McMahon off their Wild Card roster.
Boone said that he still sees McMahon as a “top-shelf” defender, but he entered Wednesday’s game with -2 Defensive Runs Saved and one Out Above Average, numbers well below career norms. Couple that with a 73 wRC+, and the $16 million man has not been a quality player, though he did hit a grand slam on Wednesday.
“I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I want him in the game and the ball hit to him in a big spot,” Boone said. “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half and lately getting it going. But through his struggles that he’s had offensively, he’s gotten a lot of big hits for us, too, along the way.”
On the subject of third base, Boone also said that he hasn’t given much thought to Jazz Chisholm Jr. trying the position again. However, he’s not ruling it out.
WHAT ABOUT OTHER INJURED ARMS?
Fernando Cruz made a rather adamant appearance in the Yankees’ clubhouse on Wednesday. The reliever, out with a partially torn UCL, repeatedly said that he refused to “accept” the diagnosis.
“I had real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” said Cruz, who isn’t considering surgery right now. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart, it’s not a partial tear.”
While it seems rather improbable that Cruz will pitch again this season, he said that that is his goal, and Boone didn’t rule out the possibility. The righty threw a touch-and-feel bullpen three days ago, and he plans to throw another bullpen on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Clarke Schmidt felt better playing catch on Wednesday than he did on Tuesday after experiencing some biceps cramping over the weekend. However, if the recently returned Tommy John patient is not a viable option by Thursday, “then we’ll probably go a different way,” Boone said, referring to the Yankees’ postseason roster plans.
Finally, Ryan Weathers isn’t expected to throw live batting practice until sometime during the Wild Card series, so he won’t be an option.
With Weathers ruled out and Schmidt’s status uncertain, it will be interesting to see how the Yankees fill out their Wild Card bullpen. On a related note, Boone said that he sees “no scenario” in which the team carries 13 pitchers for the series. They may not even roster 12, he said with so many balls up in the air.
“It depends who’s available and who’s not,” Boone said.

Anthony Volpe took grounders at third base before Wednesday’s game, and José Caballero started at third in two of the Yankees’ previous three games.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
But Ryan McMahon was back there again against the Rays as the Yankees try to get him right before the playoffs.
And Aaron Boone insisted it’s still possible.
Boone professed his confidence that McMahon remains a viable option, even as the long-slumping player has also regressed on defense.
“Defensively, I have tremendous faith in him moving forward,” Boone said Wednesday. “I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I view it as, ‘I want him in the game with the ball hit to him in a big spot.’ ”
That may be the case, but McMahon’s issues with his glove don’t just come down to a few recent errors.
According to FanGraphs, his defensive runs saved have dropped from 10 last season to -2 this year.
And scouts who have watched McMahon have noted a drop-off in his range, glove and overall fielding throughout the season.
“I get why they’re still trying to make it work,’’ one American League scout said. “The other options [at third] aren’t great, especially as you’re staring at the playoffs. But if he’s not going to be not just reliable, but stellar, then the issues with his bat are even worse.”
As Boone noted, “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half.”
Complicating matters are the lefty-swinging McMahon’s issues against left-handed pitching, which could open the door for Caballero or Amed Rosario, especially if they face a Red Sox team that’s filled with southpaws.
Caballero has done well at third but is valued for his ability to come off the bench, while the Yankees have continued to believe that Rosario, who has hit lefties well in recent years, will get back to that after having a hard time against them this season.
McMahon entered Wednesday with a .614 OPS, which ranked 224th out of 232 players with at least 350 plate appearances.
And versus lefties, McMahon has an OPS of .518, also among the lowest in the majors.
That doesn’t figure to lead to too many good matchups for McMahon.
Boone, though, said McMahon has “gotten a lot of big hits for us along the way. Defensively, not much has changed in that I view him as top-shelf over there.”
A year ago against Boston in the wild card, McMahon started just one of the three games, but then had a solid series in the ALDS against Toronto.
“We’ll try to get more out of him offensively,’’ Boone said. “Last year, he went into the postseason and right away had some big hits for us. You never know how that can switch, especially when a guy has the ability like [McMahon] does.”
As for the Volpe experiment, Boone said he wanted to get the converted shortstop over to third “a time or two” before the end of the regular season.
Volpe played three games at third with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre this season and would be “ready to go” if called upon.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – Consider it a long shot, but Giancarlo Stanton has entered the Yankees’ playoff conversation.
Down at Somerset, the slugging DH – on the injured list since April 25 – is batting against live pitching and even running the bases.
“I heard G went deep over there,’’ manager Aaron Boone said of Stanton’s “six or seven’’ at-bats Wednesday, with at least one home run.
Boone described both Stanton (calf) and Trent Grisham (hamstring) as “knocking on the door’’ in their Somerset rehab, with the lefty-hitting center fielder also hitting and running the bases.
But are they really in consideration for a Wild Card series roster spot?
“I don’t know. Anything’s possible. We’ll see,’’ Boone said Wednesday at Yankee Stadium, with his club already locked into hosting a best-of-three playoff beginning Tuesday.
Meanwhile, a day after Boone said that the Yankees weren't planning on having Aaron Judge ready for the Wild Card series due to a "moderate'' grade right calf strain, the captain told ESPN that he's planning otherwise.
Judge told reporter Jorge Castillo that he's trying "to get my body ready so I'm ready to go'' by Tuesday.
On Monday, Judge had a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection, limiting his activity.
Judge was asked by ESPN if he expected to be on the first round playoff roster replied: "I don't make the roster. I've got no idea."
Giancarlo Stanton's lengthy absence
It’s been five months since Stanton last appeared in Boone’s lineup, due to three separate calf strains – including his current right calf issue.
Due to Stanton’s DH-only status, and the makeup of the Yanks’ current roster, “you’re looking more in a pinch-hit scenario,’’ Boone said of his potential role.
“We’ll see if that’s even a realistic option,’’ said Boone. “I don’t know yet.’’
But it’s an interesting development, and something to watch if the Yanks advance deeper in October.
Again, Judge isn’t in the Yankees’ first-round playoff plans due to a calf strain that might cast him as doubtful to return this year.
Stanton’s finest moments as a Yankee have come during postseason, which adds to his intrigue; as a looming option, he’d at least give an opposing manager something else to weigh.
Advertisement
On the IL since Sept. 5, Grisham might stand a better chance at activation, given the Yanks’ lack of outfield depth.
Hard-throwing righty Carlos Lagrange is pitching at the Yanks’ Somerset camp for potential playoff roster additions, coming back from a capsular (right shoulder) strain.
Lagrange’s big arm and his potential for transitioning to an impact bullpen role was an exciting prospect for the Yanks, until his injury in late July.
As of now, “he’s in the conversation for something,’’ Boone said of Lagrange, the rookie who has yet to make a big-league appearance.
Speaking of both Stanton and Lagrange, specifically, Boone said their recent activity puts them “on the outskirts of the conversation’’ about the postseason “if nothing else.’’
Clarke Schmidt, Fernando Cruz updates
After a recent bout of biceps cramping, Clarke Schmidt’s throwing session Wednesday was “better’’ than Tuesday’s effort, per Boone.
However, “if he’s not a real viable option by (Thursday), we’ll probably go a different way,’’ Boone said of Schmidt’s diminishing chances of being on a Wild Card series roster.
Though apparently minor, this is Schmidt’s second setback since his rehab from Tommy John surgery in July 2025.
Meanwhile, right-hander Fernando Cruz (partial torn UCL) threw a bullpen session Sunday, and plans to throw again Thursday.
Cruz opted against surgery and is trying to be a postseason bullpen option.
“That’s what we’re shooting for…to be back in the next couple of weeks,’’ said Cruz, adding that, in his mind, he’s not dealing with a partial tear.
“I’m going through inflammation and real chronic irritation,’’ said Cruz, determined to pitch through his condition.
Anthony Volpe will get a look at third base
Over these next few games, Boone plans to give Anthony Volpe some playing time a third base.
It's a position he's played briefly in the minors but never in the majors, though Volpe says he feels "pretty comfortable'' in his limited experience at the hot corner.
Volpe has so far made a successful transition from shortstop to second base, and "I'll just try to be prepared'' for whatever the team needs from him defensively.
This article originally appeared on NorthJersey.com: Giancarlo Stanton a Yankees playoff option again? Latest rehab update

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees split their doubleheader against the Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday.
With one of those losses, the Rays officially clinched the AL East division and the No. 1 overall seed in the American League postseason.
This now places the Yankees in the top Wild Card spot, meaning they'll host a best-of-three series next week in the Bronx against what seems like the Boston Red Sox if the current standings hold.
Yankees Announce Anthony Volpe Decision
With New York already locked into a playoff spot, manager Aaron Boone seems like he's going to experiment with his lineup over these final five games.
However, for the second straight night, he's electing to keep infielder Anthony Volpe out of the starting lineup.
Volpe was seen pregame Wednesday evening taking reps at third base after Boone mentioned that morning that he'll play some third base this week after Jazz Chisholm Jr. returned from the IL.
That seemingly won't happen in Game 3 of the series, though, unless Volpe enters the game off the bench at some point. Ryan McMahon will start at third base.
Here's the full Yankees lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: "Yankees 9/23 B. Rice DH G. Lombard Jr. SS L. García Jr. 1B H. Ramos RF S. Jones CF J. Chisholm Jr. 2B J. Caballero LF R. McMahon 3B A. Sánchez C G. Cole SP."
Yankees 9/23
B. Rice DH
G. Lombard Jr. SS
L. García Jr. 1B
H. Ramos RF
S. Jones CF
J. Chisholm Jr. 2B
J. Caballero LF
R. McMahon 3B
A. Sánchez C
G. Cole SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 23, 2026
Volpe's Rocky 2026 Campaign
It's been a year of ups and downs for Volpe, who's in his fourth season with the Yankees.
He's appeared in 67 games at the major league level while also spending some time in Triple-A this year. He enters Wednesday hitting .244 with 51 hits, two home runs, and 26 RBIs while slugging .335 with a .655 OPS.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees’ Anthony Volpe’s audition at third comes amidst Ryan McMahon’s struggles as postseason nears
item.dc:creator: James O'Connell

item.content:encoded:
Hours before Wednesday’s meaningless game between the Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays, reporters swarmed Anthony Volpe’s locker as he was seen taking grounders at third base.
Volpe’s locker is positioned next to third baseman Ryan McMahon’s, who sat unnoticed right beside the former top prospect while he was swarmed with questions about potentially playing the hot corner.
It could be a sign of things to come, as the Yankees will be getting the infielder out there at third base — as they did during his time in the minors — at some point during the remaining five games of the regular season.
“I would say it just took a couple, like one session of earlier work, just to get used to it,” said Volpe. “And then I felt like it was pretty comfortable. … t’s definitely more similar to shortstop.”
The Bombers have nothing left to play for as the Rays celebrated winning the AL East on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium and their spot atop the Wild Card standings is locked in.
Therefore, the only value these games provide is trying new things. Volpe at third base is among the most intriguing options.
“Yeah, there’s a lot going on with things from our standpoint being settled as far as our playoff standing and position and everything,” said Boone. “There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days. Hopefully we have a lot of options to choose from, but we won’t know that until Saturday or Sunday and into Monday. …
“I’ll probably get [Volpe] in there a time or two. Just certainly want him working over there a little bit and again trying to be as flexible as possible. There’s a lot of different iterations and ways we can go going into the Wild Card series where if you went heavy position player [on the roster], you could have a lot of options throughout the game and the more position flexibility you have, the better.”
The Bombers’ left-handed heaviness has been well-documented. Boone values balance in the lineup and the Yanks haven’t had much of it.
McMahon has objectively been a weak bat since he’s arrived in New York last season. This season, the 31-year-old is slashing .209/.274/.341 with 10 homers and 35 RBI in 121 games.
Against lefties, it’s even worse.
McMahon is slashing .196/.286/.232 against southpaws this season. That doesn’t bode well entering October, while the book is out on the Yankees’ preference to face righties. Barring some crazy series of events during the final weekend of the regular season, the Yanks will likely be welcoming the Boston Red Sox into Yankee Stadium for a best-of-three Wild Card series.
The Sox are well equipped to potentially go with left-handed starters in all of three of those games. This is where Volpe could potentially come into play.
The 25-year-old has performed respectably since being recalled from Triple-A on Sept. 10. Volpe is slashing .263/.300/.395 with one homer, seven RBI and four stolen bases — reminder, the bar is very low offensively for these Yankees right now.
Against lefties on the whole in his 67 MLB games this season, Volpe owns a .680 OPS — it’s well below average, however, it’s a large improvement from McMahon. The one thing to consider, however, is the potential defensive downgrade to consider with McMahon ranking in the 80th percentile in Outs Above Average at third base.
There is certainly an October role available for Volpe to carve out this season. The third base situation is amongst the many unanswered questions for the Yanks entering the postseason.
McMahon is no shoo-in to make the postseason roster with his season-long struggles at the plate, Jose Caballero hasn’t separated himself — .666 OPS entering Wednesday — although he may be the leader in the clubhouse to get the start at the hot corner.
One could argue that far too many questions remain for the Yankees with the clock winding down this season, however, they hope to have many of them answered over these final few games.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Why José Caballero Gives Yankees Better Chance at Third Base Than Ryan McMahon in MLB Playoffs

item.content:encoded:
For much of the New York Yankees' 2026 season, there was a constant conversation about who would be the everyday shortstop. The debate surrounded Jose Caballero and Anthony Volpe for most of the year. In the end, the debate over who was better became irrelevant because George Lombard Jr. won the job.
While Caballero is currently without a position, that doesn't mean he doesn't have an opportunity to get everyday reps in the postseason. In fact, maybe the conversation of Caballero vs. Volpe could shift toward him vs. Ryan McMahon. At this point in the season, can the Yankees honestly say McMahon's defense is that much of a difference-maker when he is easily one of the worst everyday bats this organization has ever had?
It isn't hyperbole to mention that McMahon is that bad, either. According to Baseball Reference's Katie Sharp on X, 232 players have over 350 plate appearances this season. He is the only one with an OBP under .280 and a strikeout rate over 29%.
Beyond being a bad hitter, McMahon's defense has regressed. Last season, McMahon had a 7 OAA and 10 DRS. This year, he has a 1 OAA at third and -2 DRS. He can't hit, and apparently his defense — his only calling card as a player — is mediocre at best.
That is why, at this point, it wouldn't hurt to leave McMahon off the Wild Card roster. It isn't a secret that the Boston Red Sox are going to throw an amalgamation of lefties that entire series, and considering McMahon can't hit anybody no matter which side of the mound they're throwing from, Caballero makes the most sense to play every game in that series.
The difference between McMahon and Caballero
That said, Caballero hasn't been all that great this season, either. He has an 86 wRC+ and .666 OPS this year. The one thing he brings is athleticism, and he showed that against the Tampa Bay Rays. In the day game of their day-night doubleheader on Tuesday, Caballero stole second and third with ease.
The Yankees didn't score, unfortunately, but Caballero put them in the position to do so. The Yankees don't get that with McMahon.
Considering McMahon has also regressed defensively, it wouldn't be a downgrade at the hot corner anyway if the Yankees go with Caballero, who has a -1 OAA and 1 DRS at the position. It would just be one bad hitter replacing another, except Caballero is always a threat to steal and brings speed on the bases.
Going from Caballero to McMahon feels like one of the easiest decisions the Yankees have heading into the Wild Card series. At this point, McMahon does nothing better than Caballero, and given that Caballero is already one of the weakest bats in baseball, it's hard to find anything positive about his season.
That said, his ability to put pressure on the opposing teams' pitcher with his base-stealing prowess could be a differencemaker in the playoffs.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

Things took a turn on Tuesday when Jazz Chisholm returned from the 10-day injured list after suffering a thumb injury earlier in the month, reclaiming his spot at second base. item.content:encoded:
Is it possible the New York Yankees will have a larger playoff role for Anthony Volpe than expected?
Things took a turn on Tuesday when Jazz Chisholm returned from the 10-day injured list after suffering a thumb injury earlier in the month, reclaiming his spot at second base.
But will Chisholm be a permanent fixture there in the playoffs? And is it possible Anthony Volpe could get more playing time than expected?
Chisholm had yet another mental lapse on Tuesday night, failing to cover first base on a bunt. Aaron Boone expressed clear frustration with Chisholm after the game and didn't rule out the possibility of Anthony Volpe playing some second base even with Chisholm back.
Chisholm does not hit lefties well. He is slashing .221/.268/.386 against them in 2026 and owns a lifetime .663 OSP versus southpaws.
Volpe hasn't exactly lit it up against left-handers, either (.719 OPS), but he does hit lefties slightly better than Chisholm, and given how frustrated Boone appears to be with Chisholm, there appears to be a chance Volpe gets some run.
The Boston Red Sox will be the Yankees' Wild Card Series opponent. They are absolutely loaded with left-handed pitching. It's basically Sonny Gray and then a bunch of southpaws. Does that mean Chisholm will be out of luck in that short series?
Of course, it's only a three-game set, but if it does go the full three, Volpe might get starts in two of them. That seemed unheard of in early August when Volpe was demoted to Triple-A, but now, it's a legitimate possibility for the 25-year-old.
It should also be noted that Volpe has shown some playoff chops in the past, particularly during New York's run to the World Series in 2024 when he slashed .286/.407/.408 with a home run and six RBI.
Is Volpe going to be anyone's favorite option? No, but he has demonstrated that he is not afraid of the bright October lights, and it's not like Chisholm has been good enough this season to warrant a guaranteed start every night.
It's also worth noting that Volpe has done a fine job defensively at second base, registering two defensive runs saved over 93.1 innings there thus far.
Just when Yankees fans thought they may have seen the last of Volpe, the former first-round pick may surprise them with potentially significant postseason playing time. And while that may not be preferable, New York may not have any other choice.

item.description:
The glaring Ryan McMahon playoff problem has the Yankees set to once again expand Anthony Volpe’s defensive repertoire. Volpe, now at second base after transitioning from shortstop, will “probably” play third base in the team’s final five games, Yankees manager Aaron Boone told Talkin’ Yanks.

item.content:encoded:
The glaring Ryan McMahon playoff problem has the Yankees set to once again expand Anthony Volpe’s defensive repertoire.
Volpe, now at second base after transitioning from shortstop, will “probably” play third base in the team’s final five games, Yankees manager Aaron Boone told Talkin’ Yanks.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
The team is not planning to do so with Jazz Chisholm, although Boone caveated that statement with a “we’ll see” during his usual midweek interview with the podcast.
The Yankees have six days before they likely welcome the Red Sox — or the AL Central runner-up — to The Bronx for a second straight AL wild-card series and they will use this time to figure out roster construction.
Boone said after the Rays clinched the AL East on Tuesday in the nightcap of the doubleheader that he would consider experimenting with players at certain positions.
The glaring roster question centers on third base.
McMahon has become virtually unplayable due to his shaky defense as of late and horrific offense.
The veteran is hitting just .143 in 15 games since returning from the injured list, going 6-for-42 with one extra-base hit and a .217 on-base percentage.
Against a Boston team filled with lefties, McMahon, who owns a .518 OPS against southpaws this year, becomes an easy fade.
The question is where the Yankees would turn and they have Amed Rosario and Jose Caballero as potential options, although there are flaws with both.
Rosario is a bad defender this year and has not hit lefties like usual, with just a .599 OPS, and Caballero can be rather streaky offensively.
Volpe has tallied just a .695 OPS in 11 games since being recalled, which doesn’t scream must-start, but his righty bat could be needed against potential southpaws.
He also has handled second base rather well since shifting to the position earlier this month with rookie George Lombard Jr. handling shortstop.
Boone added that Lombard will remain at shortstop amid these possible changes.
The complicating factor about Volpe’s postseason role is whether the Yankees trust Chisholm — who is slashing .221/.268/.386 versus lefties — against a southpaw in a three-game series.
If Chisholm is starting, the only other starting route would be third base.
Seeing how Volpe can handle third base opens up the possibility of starting at the hot corner — although that would appear a long shot since he would have, at most, five major-league games at the position before the postseason starts — or potentially entering or shifting in the late innings.
Volpe being able to handle the position could allow the Yankees to optimize their roster in a better fashion in the late innings, with one potential example being a game in which Rosario starts.

item.content:encoded:
Updated Yankees projected Wild Card Series roster without Aaron Judge
NEW YORK - Here was the scenario these Yankees hoped to avoid, but couldn't - a triumphant Tampa Bay Rays team, celebrating their AL East title on Bronx turf.
"They've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that,'' said manager Aaron Boone, after the Rays' 6-1 victory in Tuesday's nightcap of a split doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
"Hopefully, we get another crack at them.''
That would be in a best-of-five AL Division Series, but only if the Yankees advance from a best-of-three Wild Card series, which they'll host - likely against the rival Red Sox.
With that Wild Card opponent in mind, here is our updated version of a Yankees 26-man playoff roster (12 pitchers, 14 position players), for a series that would begin on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
Rosters can be altered before each postseason round. Injured players can be replaced in-series (pitcher for pitcher, position player for position player) but the injured player is ineligible for the next playoff series.
Projected Yankees pitchers (12)
Starters (3): RHPs Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole; LHP Max Fried.
Relievers (9): RHPs David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Will Warren, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber; LHPs Ryan Weathers, Tim Hill, Brent Headrick, Carlos Rodon.
On the bubble: RHPs Clarke Schmidt.
Also available: RHPs Luis Gil, Elmer Rodriguez, Yerry de los Santos, Bradley Hanner, Carlos Lagrange; LHP Ryan Yarbrough.
Currently injured: RHPs Fernando Cruz, Angel Chivilli, Kervin Castro.
Analysis: Would the Yanks start anyone but Schlittler in Game 1?
Well, nothing's been firmly stated about the first round rotation, though Schlittler - the odds-on choice for the AL Cy Young Award - would be on normal rest for the opener.
Cole (Wednesday) and Schlittler (Thursday) will make their final regular season starts during this Rays series, though Boone mentioned limiting both starters in these tune-ups for postseason.
In the bullpen, Schmidt's recent bout of biceps cramping wasn't fully resolved as of Tuesday; he was due to be re-examined after a throwing session.
It's possible that even a slight setback takes Schmidt out of consideration for an important playoff spot, moving Michael Fulmer off the bubble and on the roster.
Rodon's eight shutout innings in Tuesday's doubleheader opener was his best effort, during an impressive stretch drive.
He'd be certain to start Game 1 or 2 of a Division Series vs. the Rays, but the Yanks might need his services - in some capacity - to advance vs. Boston, so he's now included here.
Projected Yankees infielders, utility/DH (9)
Infielders (7): Luis Garcia Jr., 1B; Paul Goldschmidt, 1B; Ben Rice, 1B-DH; Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B; George Lombard Jr., SS; Anthony Volpe, 2B-SS; Ryan McMahon, 3B.
Utility players: (2): Jose Caballero, IF-OF; Amed Rosario, 3B-2B.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Max Schuemann.
Analysis: Garcia and McMahon are slumping at the wrong time, while Chisholm - who just returned off the IL (right thumb sprain) on Tuesday - has this week to find his rhythm again at the plate.
But that trio of lefty hitters might all be starting on the bench against Boston, which could employ three lefty starters against the Yanks.
That puts Caballero in play as a third base option, with the veteran Goldschmidt (.997 OPS vs. lefties) at first base, the rookie Lombard at short, and Volpe recast as a second baseman.
Projected Yankees outfielders (3)
Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Jasson Dominguez.
Currently injured: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham.
Analysis: That's a thin outfield without Judge, whom the Yanks are not planning to have for at least the Wild Card series - per Boone - due to the captain's "moderate'' right calf strain.
It's increasingly unlikely that Grisham (strained hamstring) is available, too, by next week, and that presents a danger considering Ramos' defensive deficiencies.
For that same reason, Dominguez is on the outside. Mostly, the Yanks need the potent right-handed bats of Ramos (who has found his hitting groove) and Rosario to combat Boston's lefty pitching.
Caballero could find himself pressed into outfield duty, too.
Without Judge, "it's going to be super tough on us,'' said Ramos. "But we're going to go forward, for sure.''
Yankees' projected catchers (2)
Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: J.C. Escarra.
Analysis: Wells has been a better offensive presence after a brutal first half, and Sanchez has learned the staff and he earned much praise from Rodon for his contribution to Tuesday's game one win.
Boone has kept the Cole-Wells pairing together, and you'd still anticipate Wells getting starts vs. Boston's lefty starters throughout this opening series.

item.title: [MLB.com] Cinco factores por los que los Yankees podrían ganar sin Judge
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch
item.description: NUEVA YORK – La noticia sobre el regreso de Aaron Judge a la lista de lesionados aún estaba fresca, habiendo sido anunciada menos de una hora antes, y ya Cody Bellinger estaba imaginando cómo los Yankees podían tener éxito en la postemporada sin su capitán. Desafortunadamente para Judge y su club, han tenido mucha práctica haciendo exactamente eso esta temporada. No han tenido otra opción. "Falta Judge y duele", dijo Bellinger. "Todos sabemos que él es el mejor bateador del juego. Para nosotros
item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – La noticia sobre el regreso de Aaron Judge a la lista de lesionados aún estaba fresca, habiendo sido anunciada menos de una hora antes, y ya Cody Bellinger estaba imaginando cómo los Yankees podían tener éxito en la postemporada sin su capitán.
Desafortunadamente para Judge y su club, han tenido mucha práctica haciendo exactamente eso esta temporada. No han tenido otra opción.
"Falta Judge y duele", dijo Bellinger. "Todos sabemos que él es el mejor bateador del juego. Para nosotros aquí, nuestra mentalidad es que vamos a tener que encontrar la manera. Creo que el talento en este clubhouse habla por sí mismo. Estoy completamente seguro de que tenemos suficiente talento aquí para salir, ganar y vencer a cualquiera.
Ahora tendrán su oportunidad para demostrarlo.
El manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, confirmó el martes que Judge está lidiando con un esguince "moderado" de la pantorrilla derecha y no se espera que esté listo para una posible Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana contra los Medias Rojas, que comenzaría el 29 de septiembre.
La disponibilidad de Judge para las rondas posteriores, especialmente la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, también está en duda. Pero los Yankees necesitan llegar allí primero. Aquí hay cinco motivos por los que los Yankees, elogiados como favoritos para ganar el banderín, aún pueden llegar a la Serie Mundial incluso si Judge no regresa:
Lanzadores abridores dominantes
**
Cuando Carlos Rodón lanzó ocho entradas sin permitir carreras en la **victoria por 2-0 del martes sobre los Rays, no sólo mantuvo el champán en el clubhouse de Tampa Bay (por el momento), sino que también sirvió como un recordatorio de la mayor fortaleza de los Yankees.
Rodón podría ni siquiera abrir un partido en una posible Serie de Comodines, quedando detrás de los favoritos al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole y Max Fried. En pocas palabras, la rotación los ha mantenido a flote.
Los abridores de los Yankees han permitido dos carreras limpias o menos en 40 de 51 aperturas desde el 28 de julio, incluyendo una carrera limpia o menos en 33 de esas aperturas, acumulando efectividad de 2.50 en ese período. En general, han permitido una carrera o menos en 65 encuentros, un récord de franquicia en una sola campaña.
"Venimos a ganar cada partido, sin importar quién esté en el terreno", dijo Rodón. "Obviamente, es difícil cuando no tienes al mejor jugador del mundo en el terreno contigo. Tengo la esperanza de que vuelva. Pero... se trata simplemente de ganar juegos para nosotros.
Hay otro trueno
Esto no es el 2022, cuando los 62 jonrones de Judge establecieron un récord de la Liga Americana para una sola temporada y sirvieron como el motor indiscutible de la ofensiva. Principalmente debido a la lesión en la costilla, Judge se limitó a un promedio de .241, 18 vuelacercas y 41 impulsadas en 66 encuentros. Ben Rice asumió gran parte de la carga este año, cumpliendo con la predicción de la primavera de Boone de 39 cuadrangulares.
Bellinger sigue siendo una fuerza impactante, mientras que el aumento de la velocidad del bate del dominicano Luis García Jr. sugiere que su producción es sostenible, a pesar de una reciente caída. Mientras tanto, el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos ha mostrado poder después de un comienzo lento y se confiará en él en los playoffs contra lanzadores zurdos.
"Sabemos que somos capaces de ganar partidos", dijo Boone, quien señaló el récord de 36-24 del club desde el descanso del Juego de las Estrellas, la mayor parte del cual ocurrió sin Judge. "Nos hemos tenido que enfrentar a jugar sin muchas piezas clave en diferentes momentos y durante grandes tramos de esta campaña”.
**Los jóvenes pueden dar la cara
**
El cubano-estadounidense George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones llamaron la atención durante la reciente serie del club contra los Diamondbacks, cuando dieron jonrones con un total combinado de 872 pies calculados por Statcast contra Corbin Burnes – potentes batazos de 424 y 448 pies, respectivamente, que sugieren que se están sintiendo más cómodos en Grandes Ligas.
Ha habido algunos obstáculos durante sus primeros meses de actividad en las Mayores, con Lombard cometiendo errores en seis compromisos consecutivos en un período y Jones mostrando los swings en blanco que probablemente siempre sean parte de su juego. Pero el talento es real y nadie debería sorprenderse si alguno de los novatos brilla en un gran momento de octubre.
"Realmente sólo tenemos que jugar uno para el otro; apoyarnos mutuamente, pasar la batuta", dijo Bellinger. "Haces tu trabajo y controlas lo que puedes”.
Mejorando la salud
Mientras la situación de Judge no está clara, los Yankees están volviendo lentamente a estar completos.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. fue activado de la lista de lesionados entre los juego de la doble-jornada del martes, restaurando una presencia dinámica. Ha sido un año decepcionante en general, pero Chisholm estaba en racha en el momento de su lesión (de 46-18, .391). Los Yankees esperarán que retome eso.
Mientras tanto, Anthony Volpe aprovechó al máximo una oportunidad ante la ausencia de Chisholm, lo que podría haberle valido un lugar en el roster de playoffs, especialmente si los Yankees optan por contar con 11 lanzadores y 15 jugadores de posición en la primera ronda. Se cree que Trent Grisham está en la contienda para el roster.
"Con suerte, más personas podrán unirse y hacernos más formidables en el camino", dijo Boone.
Un bullpen reforzado
Los relevistas de los Yankees han estado entre los mejores de Grandes Ligas todo el año, pero ha habido señales preocupantes últimamente. Brent Headrick ocupa el segundo lugar en las Grandes Ligas con 79 presentaciones y ha mostrado una velocidad inconsistente. Mientras tanto, David Bednar y Paul Blackburn siguen en buena forma.
Debido a que los Yankees no tendrían por qué para a tener cinco abridores en octubre, la ayuda está en camino. Will Warren tiene programada una última apertura y luego pasará a un rol de relevista, dando al bullpen una opción intrigante de múltiples entradas. Clarke Schmidt y Ryan Weathers también están en consideración.
"Eso es lo bueno de la postemporada; los muchachos caen en diferentes roles y muchas veces pueden ser heroicos en papeles que no necesariamente imaginabas al inicio de la temporada", expresó Boone.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Aaron Boone's Anthony Volpe reveal may finally stick a fork in Ryan McMahon before Yankees playoff run

item.content:encoded:
With one six-foot-seven sized caveat, the biggest concern facing the New York Yankees as we prepare for October is third base. Ryan McMahon has proven to be too much of a liability at the plate to count on as he's sunk to a new low as the only player in the league (min. 350 plate appearances) to post a sub-.280 on-base percentage and a strikeout rate north of 29%.
Meanwhile, Amed Rosario's inability to do his one job, hit lefties, and porous glove make him an untenable alternative. It appeared as if the Yankees would just have to deal with a black hole in the lineup and/or a butcher in the field, but Aaron Boone's latest update might have a solution coming to the rescue in a strange way.
With Jazz Chisholm Jr. back in action, and apparently kissing fans, the skipper announced a new plan for Anthony Volpe: playing third base. Boone always uses qualifiers, so to be accurate, he said he'd "probably" send Volpe out the man the hot corner some time this week, so there's always a chance that the frustratingly opaque manager could change his mind. Still, it would be nice to have another option, and believe it or not, Volpe could be a decent one.
Anthony Volpe ironically could come full circle and become a Yankees savior with the proposed third base plan
There's some reason to be concerned about how Volpe can handle third base, especially due to questions about his arm. The greater fear is that if he struggles there, he'll bring those issues with him to the batter's box and scuffle on the offensive side of the ball as well.
However, the former can't-miss prospect got a decent amount of run at the hot corner during his last demotion to Scranton, and during the last month he was in Triple-A, he hit 10 homers and posted an eye-popping 1.023 OPS.
Since he's come back up, his bat hasn't been that hot, hitting .263/.300/.395. Still, that's an improvement over McMahon, and he's had a few big moments over the last few weeks, most notably his September 10 grand slam against the Colorado Rockies.
Getting him some big league reps at the position before the playoffs begin is a great way to test this out in a low-pressure environment now that New York has clinched home-field advantage against the Boston Red Sox for the upcoming AL Wild Card Series.
If it works, well, it sets up a world of possibilities. We don't want to get ahead of ourselves, but Volpe getting hot at a new position in the postseason could completely flip his career narrative. If he makes a positive impact, his confidence could soar, fueling more and more encouraging developments.
At the end of it all, he could prove to be a viable replacement for the struggling McMahon this offseason. That's huge because unless the Yankees pull off a blockbuster trade, the free agent market is barren at the hot corner. One step at a time, but this could serve as the jumping-off point for Volpe's rebirth, and we're 100% here for that.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees manager Aaron Boone provided some updates during his weekly appearance on the 'Talkin Yanks' podcast…
Volpe at the hot corner
Third base is one of the positions the Yanks still need to shore up before they kick off postseason play next week.
Ryan McMahon has struggled mightily, reaching a near unplayable level.
The Yanks will also likely face numerous lefties against the Red Sox in the Wild Card round, pushing the lefty-hitting McMahon to the bench.
In an effort to solve that problem, Boone said that he'll be testing out Anthony Volpe at the hot corner at some point over the next week.
In that scenario, George Lombard Jr. would stick at shortstop.
While Volpe has never played third in the majors, he did see some time there in the minors in an effort to increase his versatility this year.
The 25-year-old has looked much better at the plate of late, hitting .263 with a .300 OBP and seven RBI in 11 games since returning to the majors.
Cruz on the mend
Boone said that Fernando Cruz is doing "pretty well" in his recovery from a partially torn UCL.
Cruz was able to throw for the first time this week.
An MRI revealed the injury in late-August, but the righty is attempting to pitch through it and return down the stretch.
He'll likely have to undergo surgery at some point, but could play a factor with the Yanks as long as things continue progressing as planned.
The reliever pitched to a strong 3.13 ERA in 61 appearances before the injury.

item.title: [mlb.com] 5 reasons the Yankees can win without Judge
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch

Unfortunately for Judge and his club, they’ve had plenty of practice doing exactly that this season. They’ve had no choice. “Missing Judge, it hurts,” Bellinger said. “We all know he’s the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is, we’re g
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The news about Aaron Judge’s return to the injured list was still fresh, having been announced less than an hour earlier, and already Cody Bellinger was envisioning how the Yankees could succeed in the postseason without their captain.
Unfortunately for Judge and his club, they’ve had plenty of practice doing exactly that this season. They’ve had no choice.
“Missing Judge, it hurts,” Bellinger said. “We all know he’s the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is, we’re going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I’m fully confident that we have enough talent in here to go out, win and beat anybody.”
Now they’ll have their chance to prove it.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said Tuesday that Judge is dealing with a “moderate” strain of his right calf and is not expected to be ready for a potential American League Wild Card Series against the Red Sox, which would begin on Sept. 29.
Judge’s availability for subsequent rounds, especially the AL Division Series, is also in doubt. But the Yankees need to get there first. Here are five reasons why the Yankees, lauded as pennant favorites, still can reach the Fall Classic even if Judge doesn’t return:
Dominant starting pitching
Rodón might not even draw a start in a potential Wild Card Series, standing in line behind AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole and Max Fried. Simply put, the rotation has kept them afloat.
Yankees starters have permitted two earned runs or fewer in 40 of 51 starts since July 28, including one earned run or fewer in 33 of those starts, compiling a 2.50 ERA over that span. Overall, they’ve allowed one run or fewer in 65 games, a single-season franchise record.
“We come to win every game, regardless of who is on the field,” Rodón said. “Obviously it’s tough when you don’t have the best player in the world on the field with you. I’m hopeful that he’ll be back. But … it’s just about winning games for us.”
There’s other thump
This isn’t 2022, when Judge’s 62 home runs set a single-season AL record and served as the unquestioned engine of the offense. Mostly because of the rib injury, Judge was limited to a .241 average, 18 homers and 41 RBIs across 66 games. Ben Rice shouldered much of the load, fulfilling Boone’s spring prediction of 39 homers.
Bellinger remains an impactful force, while Luis García Jr.’s increased bat speed suggests his production is sustainable despite a recent slump. Meanwhile, Heliot Ramos has shown power after a sluggish start and will be leaned upon in the playoffs against left-handed pitching.
“We know we’re capable of winning games,” said Boone, who noted the club’s 36-24 record since the All-Star break, most of which occurred without Judge. “We’ve had to play without a lot of key pieces at different points and for large chunks of this season.”
The kids are all right
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones opened eyes during the club’s recent series against the Diamondbacks, when they crushed a Statcast-calculated combined 872 feet of home runs against Corbin Burnes – big-boy blasts of 424 and 448 feet, respectively, that suggested they’re growing more comfortable in The Show.
There have been growing pains across their first months of big league activity, with Lombard committing errors in six consecutive games over one span and Jones showing the swing-and-miss that will probably always be part of his game. But the talent is real, and no one should be surprised if either rookie delivers in a big October moment.
“We really just have to play for each other; lean on each other, pass the baton,” Bellinger said. “You do your job and control what you can.”
Improving health
While Judge’s outlook is cloudy, the Yankees are slowly becoming more whole.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. was activated from the injured list between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader, restoring a dynamic presence. It has been a disappointing year overall, but Chisholm was hot at the time of his injury (18-for-46, .391). The Yanks will look for him to pick up where he left off.
Meanwhile, Anthony Volpe made the most of an opportunity in Chisholm’s absence, which could have earned him a spot on a playoff roster – especially if they go with 11 pitchers and 15 position players in the first round. Trent Grisham is thought to be in play for the playoff roster.
“Hopefully more people are able to join and make us more formidable along the way,” Boone said.
A bolstered bullpen
The Yankees’ relievers have been among the league’s best all year, but there have been concerning signs of late. Brent Headrick ranks second in the Majors with 79 appearances and has seen inconsistent velocity, for example, suggesting he could benefit from a breather once the AL East is decided. David Bednar and Paul Blackburn, meanwhile, remain sharp.
Because the Yankees would have no reason to roster five starting pitchers in October, help is on the way. Will Warren is scheduled to make one more start and then transition to a relief role, giving the ’pen an intriguing multi-inning option. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are also in the mix.
“That’s the beauty of the postseason; guys fall into different roles and a lot of times can become heroic in roles you didn’t necessarily count on at the start of the season,” Boone said.

item.title: [New York Post] Jazz Chisholm Jr. makes spotty Yankees return as playoff questions loom
item.dc:creator: Dan Martin; Mark W Sanchez
item.description:
Jazz Chisholm Jr. returned to what looks like a Yankees infield competition with a hit, a walk and a defensive mistake. The second baseman was activated from the injured list for the nightcap of Tuesday’s doubleheader and got the nod at second base after Anthony Volpe — who has played well at the spot in his absence — started the first game.

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting wi
item.content:encoded:
Jazz Chisholm Jr. returned to what looks like a Yankees infield competition with a hit, a walk and a defensive mistake.
The second baseman was activated from the injured list for the nightcap of Tuesday’s doubleheader and got the nod at second base after Anthony Volpe — who has played well at the spot in his absence — started the first game.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Chisholm’s most memorable moment, though, was failing to cover first base on a safety squeeze in the 6-1 loss in The Bronx that helped the Rays clinch the division.
With one out and runners on the corners in the seventh inning and Taylor Walls at the plate, manager Aaron Boone said the Yankees were aware that a bunt would be coming “more often than not.”
And sure enough, Walls pushed a bunt toward first base, and Luis García Jr. charged, as he was supposed to, Boone said.
Chisholm started to run over but stopped, believing García would halt his charge and return to the base. Chisholm instead hovered by second base.
“He’s just gotta go [to first base] every time, and he knows that,” Boone said of Chisholm, who acknowledged the mistake.
“Next time, I’ll just keep going through,” said Chisholm, who was sidelined for two weeks after spraining his right thumb Sept. 8 and has returned to a team sorting out its infield with five games to go before the postseason.
Asked before the doubleheader if Volpe would continue to get time at second with Chisholm back, Boone said, “We’ll see.”
Chisholm went 1-for-3 with a single and a walk, while Volpe went 0-for-3 with three strikeouts in the 2-0 doubleheader opener. Entering play, Volpe had hit .286 with a .753 OPS in 10 games with Chisholm on the IL.
The Yankees also have to figure out third base, as Ryan McMahon is a mess on both sides of the ball.
José Caballero got the start there in the opener against Martinez and went 1-for-3 with a pair of stolen bases, with lefty-swinging McMahon in the lineup for the nightcap against Drew Rasmussen. McMahon went 0-for-2 with a strikeout and could not make a difficult play on a Nick Fortes chopper that reached McMahon on an in-between hop and went for an infield single.
Boone said he wanted to get “regular reps” for both Caballero and McMahon, who entered Tuesday just 6-for-40 with an OPS of .402 since returning from a sprained thumb Sept. 1.
Amed Rosario, signed in the offseason with the idea of playing third against lefties, has not produced in those situations this year, and the Yankees have mostly gone with Caballero and McMahon over the last three weeks.
To make room on the roster for Chisholm, Max Schuemann was optioned to the FCL Yankees.
Clarke Schmidt played catch Tuesday after experiencing cramping in his biceps while warming up during Sunday’s game against Arizona.
Boone said the team was awaiting word from doctors regarding the right-hander’s availability, but a source told The Post’s Joel Sherman that Schmidt still felt something in the area.
Another source said an IL stint isn’t out of the question as Schmidt is trying to earn a spot on the postseason roster after missing over a year following Tommy John surgery.
Ryan Weathers threw a bullpen session between games as he works to return from a left forearm strain, and Fernando Cruz (UCL) played catch.
The Yankees haven’t announced their playoff rotation, but Gerrit Cole has started the team’s first postseason game in every season in which he’s been healthy since he joined the organization in 2020.
The right-hander will start Wednesday and was asked by The Post how he would feel if Cam Schlittler got the start in the first game of a wild-card series this season.
“Fine by me,’’ said Cole, who had a similar reaction when there was discussion of having Nestor Cortes open the playoffs in 2022. “What matters is me trying to be my best. Whatever [Boone] thinks is good.”
Shop Yankees Merch
Giancarlo Stanton jogged in the outfield between games Tuesday. Stanton suffered his third calf strain of the season, and first in his left leg, over four weeks ago, and there remains no guarantee he returns this season… The Yankees have won at least 90 games eight times in the last nine years in which there’s been a full season. … The Yankees lost both ABS challenges early in Game 1 on Tuesday, as Ali Sánchez had a poor challenge catching in the top of the first and Heliot Ramos followed with an even worse challenge at the plate in the bottom of the inning.

item.description: On Tuesday night, the New York Yankees will play the second game of their series with the Tampa Bay Rays. They won the first (on Tuesday afternoon) by a score of 2-0. Anthony Volpe (who started at second base) finished with three strikeouts and no hits. UPDATE: The Yankees lost 6-1 in the second game. Yankees Made Volpe Change Amid Chisholm Jr. News Ahead of the second game, the Yankees announced that Jazz Chisholm Jr. has been activated off the injured list. The Yankees wrote (via X): “Prior to
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday night, the New York Yankees will play the second game of their series with the Tampa Bay Rays.
They won the first (on Tuesday afternoon) by a score of 2-0.
Anthony Volpe (who started at second base) finished with three strikeouts and no hits.
UPDATE: The Yankees lost 6-1 in the second game.
Yankees Made Volpe Change Amid Chisholm Jr. News
Ahead of the second game, the Yankees announced that Jazz Chisholm Jr. has been activated off the injured list.
The Yankees wrote (via X): “Prior to Game 2 of today’s doubleheader, the Yankees made the following roster moves: • Reinstated INF Jazz Chisholm Jr. (#13) from the 10-day injured list. • Optioned INF/OF Max Schuemann to the FCL Yankees.”
The Yankees have also announced their starting lineup.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees Game 2 9/22 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF H. Ramos RF L. García Jr. 1B S. Jones CF J. Chisholm Jr. 2B G. Lombard Jr. SS A. Wells C R. McMahon 3B M. Fried SP”
Chisholm Jr. is starting at second base, while Volpe has been removed from the lineup.
Volpe is in the middle of his fourth season with the Yankees.
He is currently batting .248 with 51 hits, two home runs, 26 RBIs, 24 runs and 11 stolen bases in 66 games this year.
Social Media Reacts To Lineup
Here’s what people were saying:
@arrocitodo: “lets seee what this night game lineup can dooooo”
@_coachtrav: “I want to see Volpe at 3B some point in the next week lol”

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Yankees Face Judge Dread
item.dc:creator: Michael Baumann
item.description: When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball.
